- **Make invalid states unrepresentable.** Design models so illegal states cannot be spelled: one enum State instead of a pile of optional stored properties (isSharing, selectedRows, shareTarget), enums for closed sets, private setters with a validating mutating method, and a strongly typed UUID instead of a String. Values: mutually-exclusive-state `enum State`; identifier `a strongly typed UUID instead of a String`. (STD-swift-07)
  - Why: Invalid combinations become unrepresentable, and a state change becomes atomic instead of a sequence of property writes you can forget to finish.
  - Sources: eks-skills-write-swift-skill.
- **Compose values into values.** Build structs from value-type stored properties so the whole type has value semantics. (STD-swift-08, should)
  - Why: A struct whose stored properties are all value types has value semantics for free, which makes undo, diffing and state restoration a single code path instead of one per property.
  - Sources: eks-skills-write-swift-skill.
- **Noncopyable types for unique ownership.** Use a noncopyable type (~Copyable) for uniquely owned things such as a file descriptor, a bank transfer or an open resource, and mark its finishing method consuming. Values: type `~Copyable`; finishing-method `consuming`. (STD-swift-09, should)
  - Why: Suppressing the copy turns 'you must not run this twice' from an assertion into a compile error and makes deinit on a struct meaningful; consuming lets the compiler prove it is the last use.
  - Sources: eks-skills-write-swift-skill.
- **Throw recoverable, trap on mistakes.** Throw for recoverable errors and use precondition or fatalError for programmer mistakes. Values: recoverable `throw`; programmer-mistake `precondition / fatalError`. (STD-swift-10)
  - Why: A failed network call keeps the program running; an out-of-bounds index means the code is wrong and must halt before the bug becomes a security issue.
  - Sources: eks-skills-write-swift-skill.
- **Errors carry their context.** Make error types enums whose cases carry context as associated values (case duplicateFriend(String), not case duplicateFriend). Values: example `case duplicateFriend(String)`. (STD-swift-11, should)
  - Why: The context is the whole point of the error.
  - Sources: eks-skills-write-swift-skill.
- **guard for errors, if let to unwrap.** Use guard for error conditions and if let for the ordinary unwrap. (STD-swift-12, should)
  - Why: guard forces the exit path.
  - Sources: eks-skills-write-swift-skill.
- **Typed throws only internally.** Use typed throws (throws(MyError)) only for internal functions, error-forwarding generic code and constrained environments, and untyped throws for public API. Values: internal `throws(MyError)`; public-api `throws`. (STD-swift-13, should)
  - Why: Boxing any Error can be too costly in constrained environments, while untyped throws keeps your freedom to change a public error type later.
  - Sources: eks-skills-write-swift-skill.
- **Force-unwrap only with a stated invariant.** Force-unwrap only where you can state the invariant, and prefer a failing #require or precondition with a message over a bare !. (STD-swift-14)
  - Why: Swift error handling is about making the failure paths visible.
  - Sources: eks-skills-write-swift-skill.
- **Main actor first, then step down.** Start every app entirely on the main thread and add concurrency only in this order, without skipping steps: async/await to hide latency (network, disk); @concurrent for your own expensive work only after Instruments (Time Profiler, hangs) shows a hang and the code cannot be made faster without concurrency; an actor only when too much main-actor state forces tasks to hop back constantly. Values: step-1 `single-threaded on the main actor`; step-2 `async/await`; step-3 `@concurrent (after Instruments shows a hang)`; step-4 `actor`. (STD-swift-15)
  - Why: Single-threaded code goes a long way and most apps never need to leave it; concurrency has real cost (task allocation, scheduling and reasoning), and this is where agents go wrong most often because the model changed in Swift 6.2.
  - Sources: eks-skills-write-swift-skill.
- **Enable Approachable Concurrency everywhere.** Turn on the Approachable Concurrency build setting in every Swift project. Values: build-setting `Approachable Concurrency`. (STD-swift-16)
  - Why: It dramatically reduces the number of concurrency errors you will see.
  - Sources: eks-skills-write-swift-skill.
- **MainActor default isolation for app modules.** Set Default Actor Isolation to MainActor for app and UI-facing modules (in a package: swiftSettings: [.defaultIsolation(MainActor.self)]). Values: Default Actor Isolation `MainActor`; package `swiftSettings: [.defaultIsolation(MainActor.self)]`. (STD-swift-17)
  - Why: It is the default for new app projects in Xcode 26, and it deletes most of your @MainActor annotations.
  - Sources: eks-skills-write-swift-skill.
- **Libraries ship nonisolated APIs.** Never set main-actor-by-default on a general-purpose library; make its APIs nonisolated (nonisolated on a type covers all its members, Swift 6.1+) rather than @MainActor or @concurrent, so clients decide where work runs. Values: library-api-isolation `nonisolated`; not `@MainActor, @concurrent`. (STD-swift-18)
  - Why: nonisolated runs wherever it is called from, which makes it the right default for library APIs because the caller decides.
  - Sources: eks-skills-write-swift-skill.
- **@concurrent moves heavy work off-main.** Do not count on async to leave the current actor: when your own CPU-heavy work has to leave the main thread (after profiling, STD-swift-15), mark it @concurrent (@concurrent func … async), not Task.detached or DispatchQueue.global(). Values: move-off-main `@concurrent func … async`; not `Task.detached, DispatchQueue.global()`. (STD-swift-19)
  - Why: In Swift 6.2 an async function runs where it was called from, while @concurrent always switches to the concurrent thread pool.
  - Sources: eks-skills-write-swift-skill.
- **No tasks for trivial work.** Do not spawn a task for trivial work such as reading a UserDefaults value. (STD-swift-20)
  - Why: A child task for that costs more than it saves.
  - Sources: eks-skills-write-swift-skill.
- **One task per end-to-end operation.** Put work that must happen in order in one task and give independent operations separate tasks. (STD-swift-21, should)
  - Why: The runtime can then interleave the independent operations.
  - Sources: eks-skills-write-swift-skill.
- **Nothing carried across an await.** Re-check your assumptions after every await; never hold a lock or a blocking primitive (DispatchSemaphore, NSCondition) across one, and never rely on thread-local storage across one; restructure instead. Values: never-across-await `locks, DispatchSemaphore, NSCondition, thread-local storage`. (STD-swift-22)
  - Why: await is a suspension point that breaks atomicity: state can change while you are suspended, and you may resume on a different thread.
  - Sources: eks-skills-write-swift-skill.
- **Actor methods are transactions.** Mutate actor state only in synchronous methods, keep async actor methods thin and consistent at every await, and after an await re-check state such as a cache (or dedupe the in-flight work) before writing it. (STD-swift-23)
  - Why: Actors guarantee mutual exclusion, not transactions: between two awaits other work runs, so check cache, await download, write cache lets two tasks both miss, both download, and the second clobber the first.
  - Sources: eks-skills-write-swift-skill.
- **Never use actors for ordering.** When work must run in order, use a task or an AsyncStream, not an actor. (STD-swift-24)
  - Why: Actors are not FIFO: they run highest-priority work first, precisely to avoid priority inversion.
  - Sources: eks-skills-write-swift-skill.
- **Isolate shared mutable state.** Hold shared mutable state in an actor or a @MainActor class, not a class plus a lock you must remember. Values: use `actor, or @MainActor class`; not `class + a lock you must remember`. (STD-swift-25, should)
  - Why: A class plus a lock is only safe while every caller remembers the lock; an actor or a @MainActor class isolates its state, which is also why both are implicitly Sendable.
  - Sources: eks-skills-write-swift-skill.
- **Write Sendable on public types.** Write Sendable explicitly on every public type you mean clients to share across isolation domains. (STD-swift-26, should)
  - Why: Public types never get inferred sendability: marking one Sendable is a promise to your clients, so Swift makes you write it.
  - Sources: eks-skills-write-swift-skill.
- **Model classes non-Sendable on purpose.** Keep most model classes neither @MainActor nor Sendable (a shared model class is non-Sendable or @MainActor, never Sendable plus manual locking), and make one nonisolated rather than Sendable when it must leave the main actor. (STD-swift-27, should)
  - Why: Staying non-Sendable on purpose prevents half the model being mutated on the main thread while the other half is mutated in the background.
  - Sources: eks-skills-write-swift-skill.
- **Stop touching what you send.** When you send a non-Sendable object to another isolation domain, make every mutation before the hand-off and never touch it afterwards. (STD-swift-28)
  - Why: Sending is allowed as long as the sender stops using it; touching it afterwards is the error.
  - Sources: eks-skills-write-swift-skill.
- **@Sendable only across domains.** Mark a function type @Sendable only when it genuinely crosses isolation domains. (STD-swift-29, should)
  - Why: Closures capture state too.
  - Sources: eks-skills-write-swift-skill.
- **Unchecked promises are a last resort.** Use @unchecked Sendable only on types with real internal synchronization (a Mutex or a lock), and nonisolated(unsafe) on a global only as a last resort, never to silence a warning. (STD-swift-30)
  - Why: Both are promises the compiler cannot check.
  - Sources: eks-skills-write-swift-skill.
- **Fix data races by not sharing.** Fix a data-race error by working down this list: stop sharing (move the object into a local so each concurrent job gets its own); make it a Sendable value type; isolate it to an actor (the main actor or your own); only then use Mutex/Atomic from the Synchronization module (stored in let properties) or @unchecked Sendable. Values: 1 `don't share it`; 2 `Sendable value type`; 3 `isolate it to an actor`; 4 `Mutex / Atomic (in let properties) or @unchecked Sendable`. (STD-swift-31)
  - Why: Not sharing is the fix for the overwhelming majority of real errors.
  - Sources: eks-skills-write-swift-skill.
- **Globals: let before locks.** Make a global or static variable safe in this order of preference: a let; @MainActor; a Mutex; nonisolated(unsafe). Values: 1 `let`; 2 `@MainActor`; 3 `Mutex`; 4 `nonisolated(unsafe)`. (STD-swift-32, should)
  - Why: Global and static variables are the most common source of errors.
  - Sources: eks-skills-write-swift-skill.
- **Bridge callback APIs to the main actor.** Annotate delegate protocols you own with @MainActor; for ones you do not own, mark the method nonisolated and use MainActor.assumeIsolated { } (or @preconcurrency on the conformance), and use @preconcurrency import only to silence sendability warnings from a module that has not migrated yet. (STD-swift-33, should)
  - Why: assumeIsolated asserts rather than hopping, so it traps loudly instead of racing silently; @preconcurrency import is temporary, and the warnings come back, correctly, once the module migrates.
  - Sources: eks-skills-write-swift-skill.
- **Prefer structured tasks for children.** Run concurrent children as structured tasks: async let for a fixed, statically known number, withTaskGroup for a dynamic number (iterating results as they land), and withDiscardingTaskGroup when children return nothing, not N unstructured Tasks or a withTaskGroup you never drain. Values: fixed-count `async let`; dynamic-count `withTaskGroup`; no-results `withDiscardingTaskGroup`. (STD-swift-34)
  - Why: Structured tasks cannot outlive their block, are awaited automatically, and inherit cancellation, priority and task-local values; withDiscardingTaskGroup frees each child's resources immediately and cancels siblings on the first error.
  - Sources: eks-skills-write-swift-skill.
- **Task { } only when no scope fits.** Open a Task { } only when the work's lifetime does not fit a scope (a delegate callback, a button tap, a view appearing), inside the synchronous callback rather than making the callback async, and manage its cancellation yourself. Values: use `Task { } inside the callback`; not `making the callback async`. (STD-swift-35, should)
  - Why: It inherits actor isolation and priority, but unstructured tasks give you none of the automatic cancellation, awaiting or scoping of structured ones.
  - Sources: eks-skills-write-swift-skill.
- **Almost never use Task.detached.** Almost never use Task.detached; if you need a detached root, put a task group inside it rather than detaching repeatedly. (STD-swift-36)
  - Why: It inherits nothing: not isolation, not priority, not task-locals.
  - Sources: eks-skills-write-swift-skill.
- **Check cancellation before expensive work.** Check Task.isCancelled or call try Task.checkCancellation() before starting expensive work, in synchronous helpers too. (STD-swift-37)
  - Why: Cancellation is cooperative: cancelling sets a flag; it stops nothing.
  - Sources: eks-skills-write-swift-skill.
- **Cancellation handlers need real locks.** For suspended work such as an AsyncSequence's next(), use withTaskCancellationHandler and protect the state it touches with an atomic or a lock, not an actor. (STD-swift-38)
  - Why: The handler runs immediately and concurrently with the body, and you cannot guarantee ordering on an actor.
  - Sources: eks-skills-write-swift-skill.
